full_read_priority1.quote: More recently, studies have attended to broader, longitudinal crowdfunding dynamics, linking pre-campaign efforts to build community with campaign outcomes (e.g., Murray et al., 2020) and linking campaign outcomes with entrepreneurial ventures' post-campaign success in delivering their products and/or services (Murray & Fisher, 2023).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Contribution to crowdfunding literature. Not assigned to this paper; noted under step 5. The cited Murray, Kotha & Fisher (2020) is the lead.
full_read_priority1.why: A pointer only: it names pre-campaign community building, not a founder's existing following, and has nothing on chance.

full_read_priority1.quote: Entrepreneurial intention emerges as platform users become aware of the attention and appreciation that they receive (through their posts and their general engagement) from other platform users, realizing that they can appropriate the value they generate for others by monetizing the content produced.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Panel of 20,538 YouTube creators on the YTtalk forum. Leisure passion alone lowers the odds of stating an intent to monetise; endorsement (likes) from the community raises it. The opening example is a YouTuber who gained 3000 subscribers before deciding to make it a career. The outcome measured is intention (a post in the monetisation forum), not a venture launched to the followers. The endorsers are forum peers, not the creator's own audience.
full_read_priority1.why: Close but not the same idea. It says a following built through a hobby can turn into a business intention ('unintentional entrepreneurship'). It does not say the founder launched a venture to a ready audience, and it never treats the audience as an asset used at launch. If anything it points to role-02 (accidental founder) plus outcome-40 (proof of demand) before founding. It is the best held source for a code, but it would need a second paper that states launching to an existing following. Quotes copied from the library Markdown; only extraction artefacts (doubled spaces, spaced apostrophes) were normalised.

full_read_priority2.paper: Johnson, Short, Chandler & Jordan (2022) JBV Insights
full_read_priority2.quote: The limited research to date suggests that these platforms provide an arena for creative personalities to leverage their followers for both on-platform and off-platform entrepreneurial success (Ashman et al., 2018; Cutolo and Kenney, 2021).
full_read_priority2.in_context: A short research-agenda note (no data, no chance angle). Its closest line, summarising Ashman et al. (2018) on p. 3, says contentpreneurs 'can leverage their success as a micro-celebrity within the platform to pursue off-platform entrepreneurship'. Off-platform income is listed as endorsements, sponsorships and personal branding (Table 3, s. 4.2).
full_read_priority2.why: It names a following as something a creator brings to later off-platform ventures, which is the theme's asset. But it is about monetising the following itself (ads, sponsorship, branded goods), not about launching a separate venture to followers who were already there. It reports this second-hand, from a review of four papers. That idea is distinct from background-16, which covers known people; a mass of strangers who follow you is not 'existing ties'. If the theme is adopted, frame it as an asset already held at launch (closer to background-12) rather than as a chance event. Leans on it only.

full_read_priority2.quote: Our data suggest entrepreneurs seeking to mobilize financial resources via crowdfunding devote significant time to community building - that is, establishing psychological bonds between individuals who possess domain-relevant knowledge and the emergent venture - prior to the launch of their campaigns.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Eight matched Kickstarter ventures. Successful founders build a pre-launch community deliberately, for this product: Lens/S's list of about 300 followers (p. 968). An unsuccessful founder (Lens/U) already had 'about 2,000 followers' on Facebook and launched to them, raising $438 from six backers (p. 970). The authors conclude that 'indiscriminately notifying all existing ties does not seem to effectively convert them into resource providers' (p. 971).
full_read_priority2.why: The audience here is built on purpose for the campaign, not held before the venture, and nothing about it is chance. The paper's useful point for the theme is a boundary: a ready-made general following (Lens/U) did not by itself turn into funding, while a following tied to the product's field did. That argues for coding the audience as a resource only when the founder says it was used. It does not support a stand-alone code. Closest existing code: background-16 (known ties), which Murray's 'invigorating specific extant ties' sharpens rather than widens.

full_read_priority2.quote: As this quote illustrates, external validation provided a powerful stimulus for entrepreneurs to turn their aspirational identities into real ones and initiate full-time ventures.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Pop-up diners become a local following before the restaurant opens: 'you guys need to open a place, we'll come support it' (Restaurant chef #5, p. 197). In the Figure 2 codes (p. 194), 'Strangers started to come as diners instead of just friends and family'. In the discussion (p. 202) the author adds 'skilled hobbyists who use online platforms such as YouTube to acquire professional contracts'.
full_read_priority2.why: The following is built by an earlier side venture (the pop-up), and its role in the paper is validation that triggers the identity shift, not launching to a ready audience. The YouTube line names the phenomenon only in passing. That fits existing codes for the event (trigger-24 unexpected market signal; outcome-40 proof of demand) better than a new audience code.

full_read_priority2.paper: Ashman, Patterson & Brown (2018) 'Don't forget to like, share and subscribe': Digital autopreneurs in a neoliberal world, Journal of Business Research 92, 474-483
full_read_priority2.quote: Some uploaders quickly realized that if a video clip garners attention, they could use its currency as a vehicle to promote themselves, and that is precisely what has happening in recent years.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Background section. The one case of launching a separate venture to an existing following (Ferragni's blog and social media enabling 'a global brand') is a press example the authors cite, not their finding. Their YouTubers' venture is the channel itself; the paper is a Foucauldian critique of their precarity, and no following is tied to chance.

full_read.theme: Skills used to build, not to see
full_read.page: unknown; in the section 'A Model of the Decision to Exploit Opportunities', very likely p. 379 (estimated, not verified)
full_read.in_context: The quote is exact. It is the bridge sentence in an RBV argument: a valuable new product (known customer demand) is not enough; to exploit it the firm also needs enabling technologies, managerial capability and stakeholder support. The paper is a conjoint study of incubator CEOs deciding WHEN to begin full-scale exploitation. It does separate exploitation from discovery, and it treats the team's skills and experience as an exploitation resource. But it never mentions chance or unexpected events. The capability is the management team's and the firm's, not the founder's personal skill, failed-venture lessons or knack. So it supports the general split (resources for exploiting vs. for discovering) but not the theme of skills used to build after a chance event.

better_quote.quote: Managerial capability refers to a firm's skills, knowledge, and experience to be able to handle difficult and complex tasks in management and production.

full_read.distinct: Closest code: 'Relevant expertise' (expertise lets the founder SEE the value of the event). The theme is distinct from it, since here skills are used to exploit, not to recognise. It also overlaps 'Working with what was at hand' (existing skills combined, with no unexpected event). Choi & Shepherd give a general resource-based reason for the build-side split, but no serendipity-specific backing.

full_read.theme: Skills used to build, not to see
full_read.in_context: The paraphrase is accurate. The sentence reads: 'Interactions among individuals can bring to one person's attention discoveries another person considers insignificant, makes it more likely skills needed to exploit a discovery are present, and reduces groupthink (Yaqub, 2018).' It is one reason, borrowed from Yaqub, inside the argument for H1 (improvisation leads to serendipity). It concerns OTHER people's skills in a group (collective improvisation), not the founder's own experience. On the exploitation side, the paper's model uses informal structure, not skills. Skills come up again only as a future moderator (human capital for discovery, absorptive capacity for conversion).

better_quote.quote: organizations' absorptive capacity (Hughes et al., 2018) may enhance its ability to convert serendipitous opportunities into improved performance.

full_read.distinct: Same as above: distinct from 'Relevant expertise', which is about recognising. Fultz & Hmieleski split discovering from exploiting serendipity (the title, and H3 vs H4), which supports the build-side idea, but the skills point is secondary and team-level. Use it as 'leans on' support alongside a stronger source, not as the backing paper.

full_read.theme: Skills used to build, not to see
full_read.in_context: The sentence 'there are skills that have been associated with the capacity to transform the unexpected into a valuable discovery: these are preparedness and competence' is on p. 325. The paper backs it straight away with Pasteur's 'chance favours only the prepared mind', which is about observation, i.e. seeing. So it does not separate skills for building from skills for seeing. themes.existing_code_overlap: 8.3 'Only clear in hindsight' (account-18) is about an event that seemed minor and later proved a turning point; Dimov separates that from the point here, that the whole path looks prescient and linear only when read backward. account-01 'Told as if planned' covers the smoothing itself, but there the founder tells the story as planned; here the founder remarks that it only looks planned afterwards. account-01 is also excluded from level-1 coding.
themes.summary: Dimov (2011) states the idea plainly: read backward from success, a venture's path looks prescient and inevitable, while forward it was groping. Because account-01 already covers smoothing done by the founder, the clean options are to add Dimov to account-01 and note the founder's own remark as a case of it, or, if it recurs, add a level-1 code for the founder flagging hindsight coherence.

full_read.page: Quote 1: p. 57 (it ends the first page, just before the '57' marker). Quote 2: p. 58, probably (it could run onto p. 59; not verified)
full_read.in_context: Both quotes are exact and fairly read. They frame the Chegg case: the CEO's TV account ('a lot like Netflix, but for college textbooks', a problem he saw as a student) is a smoothed story. Behind it lay a Craigslist-style marketplace that failed, an acquisition, a move to California and a pivot copied from BookRenter. Dimov says the 'checkered past was fading away under a new narrative', and that reading an opportunity backward makes 'discovery' seem natural while living it forward is 'groping'. He clearly states the idea that a path looks destined only in hindsight. But he states it as a bias of observers and narrators (scholars, the media, a new CEO). He does not say the founder remarks on it; in his only example the founder is the one doing the smoothing.

better_quote.quote: The company's fascinating history and checkered past was fading away under a new narrative as laid out in a feature article in the New York Times (Helft, 2009).

full_read.distinct: Closest code: 'Told as if planned' (the founder tells a chance-filled path as an orderly plan). Dimov's sentences back that code as well as, or better than, the new theme. Nothing in Dimov backs the distinctive part of the theme (the founder SAYING the arc only looks planned afterwards). 'Only clear in hindsight' is about one event's significance, which is different. Recommendation: cite Dimov for 'Told as if planned' (or for a merged hindsight-smoothing code). Do not treat him as backing a separate founder-reflexive code. Other usable sentences: 'Implicit in these studies ... is a narrative of the entrepreneur as a prescient progenitor following a hidden but linear path.' (p. 58, probable) and 'They acknowledge that the retrospectively narrated inevitability of a particular opportunity has no empirical content.' (page unknown, section 'Studying Venture Ideas').

full_read_priority1.quote: From such a perspective, the creative imaginings of entrepreneurs about the future shapes what facets of the past they 'discover' (Garud et al., 2010).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Section 5.2 (implications for entrepreneurs), on the temporal facet of narratives: past, present and future are mutually constituted, so entrepreneurs reshape the past they recall. Section 4.2.2 (p. 1182) adds that entrepreneurs re-sequence events so a story 'makes sense'. This is a conceptual review, not a study of founder accounts.
full_read_priority1.why: The paper says narratives re-order and re-select the past to fit present aims, which is the general mechanism behind account-01 'Told as if planned'. It never says that a founder remarks that the path only looks like a planned arc in hindsight. It gives no ground for separating the theme from account-01 or account-18; at most it is background for account-01.

full_read_priority2.quote: This description is opus operatum, with much of the messiness, wrong turns, waiting, ambiguity, and my own stupidity, ignorance and confusion-missing.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Gartner, using Bourdieu's opus operatum (sense-making after the process is over) vs modus operandi (while still in it), remarks that his own account of how the special issue came about leaves out the mess. Elsewhere he says founders' classroom stories typically follow a 'rite of passage' from naive to sophisticated entrepreneur (p. 618), and stories are never 'the whole story'.
full_read_priority2.why: The exact idea (a narrator remarking that a path looks orderly only afterwards) is there, but it is the editor about an editorial project, not a founder about a venture; the founder-story remarks concern genre and omission, not a founder noticing hindsight smoothing. Dimov already states the theme; Gartner could be cited as background. account-01 covers smoothing itself; account-18 is about a single event.

full_read_priority2.quote: Since people are the heroes of their own stories, they may reduce the roles of others or downplay disappointments.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Limitations: life stories are retrospective sense-making. The findings (p. 1181) also note that founders in the 'obvious choice' group built plots 'to demonstrate that their actions were purposeful and directed'.
full_read_priority2.why: Noted under step 5. A narrative-analysis paper that says retrospective accounts smooth the path, but as the researchers' caveat, not founders remarking that the path only looks planned afterwards. Does not meet the theme.

full_read_priority1.quote: The social function of this switch appears to be linked to 'normalization', reframing failure as a natural part of R&D projects rather than a result of misconduct.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Analysis of Switch 10 (Conspiracy to Zeitgeist). The narrator's own words just before (same page): 'When you do research like what we do, you have to accept failure as a common thing in our field.' The Zeitgeist type (p. 1623) is defined as tracing failure to 'institutionalized practices' that narrators acknowledge as 'normal'; Table 3 quotes include 'bricolage is a common practice in this field' and 'it is really rare that a project meets all its outcomes'.
full_read_priority1.why: This is the theme's idea in an account-of-failure paper: the setback is told as a normal hazard of the field, which is neither luck (8.1) nor own effort (8.5), and not a fortunate reframe (account-19). Caveats a coder must weigh: (1) the setting is a corporate collaborative R&D project aimed at a spin-off, the narrators are employees and partner CEOs, and this narrator is an intern; the idea carries over to founders but the evidence is not from founders; (2) Zeitgeist also includes partial self-blame, so the new code should require that the founder frames the setback as ordinary for the trade, whether or not they also take some blame. Mantere et al. (2013), which the paper builds on and which studies founders of failed ventures, is the stronger source to fetch (not held).

full_read_priority1.quote: In this way, backers become accustomed to the ups and downs often associated with creating a new product and see the venture as being able to overcome obstacles.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Effect of the 'normalizing setbacks and resolutions' practice, which the paper defines (p. 20) as 'ongoing efforts to foster faith, confidence, and understanding' through disclosing positive and negative events, recounting perseverance, and detailed language, in real-time Kickstarter updates to backers. The authors themselves hold (p. 3) that 'operational legitimacy threats are a routine part of developing and delivering a new product'.
full_read_priority1.why: Close but not the same idea. It is a live communication practice aimed at backers' legitimacy judgements, not a founder's account that attributes a setback to the normal hazards of the trade. One of its three parts, 'recounting perseverance', credits effort, which the theme excludes. That setbacks are routine is the authors' claim about events. It could be a secondary source if a new code is built on Jabbouri et al. or Mantere et al.

full_read_priority1.quote: Ucbasaran and colleagues, for example, found that entrepreneurs who had experienced significant venture failures were not less confident or likely to shy away from entrepreneurial opportunities but instead exhibited similar or greater amounts of overconfidence and venture keenness than their successful counterparts; the 'failed' entrepreneurs viewed failure as an 'entrance fee for entrepreneurship' (Ucbasaran et al., 2006: 24).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Literature review on the functionality of failure. Elsewhere (p. 80) the paper notes that in some cultures failure is 'deemed acceptable or normal'; its findings are about how newspapers and regions attribute whole-venture failure to mistakes or misfortunes.
full_read_priority1.why: The 'entrance fee' idea, that failure is a normal cost of being an entrepreneur, is near the theme, but it is cited secondhand, concerns failure of the whole venture rather than a setback, and is about willingness to try again rather than how a setback is explained. The paper's own two-way scheme (mistake versus misfortune) has no 'normal hazard' category. Ucbasaran et al. (2006) is the lead.

full_read_priority2.quote: Moreover, failure due to inexperience was commonly portrayed as an inevitable stage in the growth process of becoming a proper entrepreneur.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Inside the Catharsis narrative (founder accepts personal blame and has learned). Elsewhere Hubris and Zeitgeist narratives 'normalized the past behaviors of the narrator as something that anyone would have done' (p. 470) and Table 3 lists 'constructing failure as a common occurrence' (p. 470). Fate and Mechanistic narratives treat failure as bad luck or meaningless.
full_read_priority2.why: Each normalising move is tied either to personal responsibility and learning (Catharsis), to collective folly of the era (Hubris/Zeitgeist), or to bad luck (Fate). None is a setback told as an ordinary hazard of the trade that credits neither luck nor effort. Also whole-venture bankruptcy, not a setback within a running venture. Castelló et al. (2023) states it far more directly.

full_read_priority2.quote: Yet, because failure is pervasive, entrepreneurs also normalize failure as an intrinsic element of entrepreneurship.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Shielding narrative, discursive practice 'Shielding one's own identity by normalizing failure'. Table 3 (p. 9) sub-practice 'Showing failure as natural, always happening', with a founder saying 'There will absolutely be one. That's just business, that's just the way it is.' Discussion (p. 16): 'failure happens to everyone and is part of the entrepreneurship process'. 49 founders who moved on to new ventures.
full_read_priority2.why: Founder-level account of failure as a normal part of the trade, analysed as its own practice separate from misfortune (luck) and from accepting responsibility (effort/learning). No v3 code covers it; account-19 needs a positive reframe. Caveat: about venture failure, not smaller setbacks, and in the shielding narrative it sits beside victim-of-misfortune talk, so the code needs a rule that the founder neither calls it bad luck nor takes the blame.

themes.existing_code_overlap: Closest is condition-32 'Slack time' (discretionary time lets people explore; rushing precludes it), and condition-37 'Attention load and multitasking'. Slack time is about spare time helping chance; it does not cover a competing job or deadline that limits time and shapes what was done or lets the venture slip, so the theme is the other side of slack time rather than a duplicate. It could be merged into Slack time as its negative pole instead of becoming a new code.
themes.summary: Kappe et al. (2025), read in full, state that hybrid entrepreneurs manage both roles under time constraints and that the clash can hurt venture performance and stifle growth, which is the core of the theme. The link to chance is only leaned on: Cunha et al. (2010) say tight deadlines with free space help unexpected opportunities surface, so the theme may sit best as the negative pole of 'Slack time'.

full_read.page: e00564, p. 1 (Introduction) for 'Hybrid entrepreneurs must manage both roles under time constraints'; e00564, p. 5 (Discussion) for the 'stifled as they seek to grow' sentence. Claim gave no page.
full_read.in_context: Quote is exact but is a scene-setting sentence citing Urbig et al. (2021). The paper is a survey of 117 German hybrid entrepreneurs; its outcome is satisfaction with the wage job, not the venture. Time is treated as a finite resource the founder allocates deliberately ('actively decide how to divide their time', p. 3); more venture time shifts conflict into the job. The venture-performance link appears only as a cited claim (Nambisan and Baron, 2021) and as a motivating line in the Discussion; the authors say they did not measure venture outcomes. Nothing in the paper links time constraints to chance, luck, unexpected events or opportunity recognition (zero hits for chance/luck/unexpected/sudden). So it does not even back 'time limits shaped the venture' empirically, let alone 'time limits made chance more or less likely to matter'. At most it is background that a day job competes with the venture for time.

better_quote.quote: Time resources allocated to one role are no longer available to the other, which can lead to inter-role conflict

full_read.distinct: No existing chance code is close; the theme is a condition, and this paper offers no link to chance. Not usable as backing for a serendipity condition; at best a citation that a day job limits venture time.

full_read_priority1.quote: When work is interrupted by this type of sudden break in expectations, workers are starved of time rather than granted idle time, and thus, we would not expect an increase in creative performance (Baer and Oldham 2006, Elsbach and Hargadon 2006, Baird et al. 2012, Mochi and Madjar 2018).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Speculative aside in the theoretical implications: a positive surprise such as a demand shock that speeds work up would block incubation because workers must keep tending the primary task. Not tested.
full_read_priority1.why: States the negative pole (no time, no incubation) only as a conjecture about employees' idea generation, not about a job or deadline limiting what a founder did or letting a venture slip. Supports folding the theme into Slack time as its negative pole rather than a new code.

full_read_priority1.quote: To the extent individuals have flexibility when they report back to work (either in the original position or a less physically demanding post), more stringent reforms reduce the time available to experiment with entrepreneurship (Boden & Ruser, 2003; Meyer et al., 1995).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Introduction, stating the contribution to the slack-time literature: an earlier return to the wage job leaves less time to try entrepreneurship. Repeated on p. 357 ('shorter recovery periods constrain the time available to explore entrepreneurial opportunities').
full_read_priority1.why: States that a competing job cutting free time lowers venture entry, but only as a proposed mechanism behind an aggregate effect; says nothing about time limits shaping what founders did or letting an existing venture slip. Supports a negative pole on Slack time.

full_read_priority1.paper: Theunissen, Kensbock, Schüler, Baum & Gerards (2026) JOMS
full_read_priority1.quote: By contrast, shortening the duration of parental leave is likely to bring women back into wage employment sooner (Lalive et al., 2014), shortening the important transitional phase after childbirth and restricting mothers' capacities to detect and evaluate new business opportunities.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Hypothesis 1 argument, then tested: a 2001 German reform that shortened paid leave cut mothers' odds of becoming self-employed by about 17% (regression discontinuity, GSOEP), and a conjoint experiment found leave duration, not money, raised self-employment intent. The introduction (p. 2467) adds that some mothers 'may defer entrepreneurship due to the competing demands of caregiving and work (Jayawarna et al., 2021)', and p. 2473 that time pressure makes people 'stick to routine actions'.
full_read_priority1.why: A competing job (return to wage work) limiting the time to detect and evaluate opportunities, with causal evidence, about would-be founders. That is the theme's core idea for the start of a venture. It does not cover deadlines shaping what was done inside a running venture or a venture slipping, and it is a resource argument rather than a chance one. Best used as the negative pole of drafted condition-32 (Slack time) if that code is adopted, not as a separate code.

full_read_priority1.quote: McBirnie (2008) also notes contextual factors that can influence this willingness, including the environment and time pressures.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Willingness to follow up encountered information; the refined model also lists 'perceived or actual time constraints' and 'perceived urgency or importance of the pre-encounter task' as factors (ms pp. 11, 14). This is the negative pole of slack time for information users, not a competing job or deadline shaping a venture.
full_read_priority1.why: Supports treating time pressure as the negative pole of Slack time (condition-32) rather than a new code; not about founders, so weak support only.

full_read_priority2.quote: In brief, if one is a chef only once or twice a month, he or she misses the repeated practice and feedback necessary to sustain a stable new identity.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Part-time founders keep day jobs, and pop-ups fit around them ('compatible with what I was doing as a full-time job', p. 195). Some took 5 to 7.5 years to go full time (p. 202-203).
full_read_priority2.why: Time limited by a competing job shapes and slows the venture, which is the theme's negative pole. But the paper links it to identity formation, not to chance. It fits the plan to treat the theme as the negative pole of condition-32.

full_read_priority2.quote: Without time, women may not have the capacity to break existing behavioral patterns, scan the environment, or simply develop a plan for the future.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Discussion, 'Time as an entrepreneurship-relevant resource': women have 'more limited access to a key resource for entrepreneurial action-time'. Also p. 1171 (citing Jayawarna et al. 2021): mothers 'are more likely to exit their businesses given incompatible demands between the time required to generate sufficient returns and their caring responsibilities'; p. 1191: parental leave 'may become a barrier for development and growth once a business is operating'; Moa could not take time off her business (p. 1189).
full_read_priority2.why: States that competing demands that eat time limit what (would-be) founders can notice, plan and do, and (via the cited Jayawarna finding and the Moa case) can make the venture slip or exit. This is the negative pole of slack time; it supports adopting condition-32 as a two-pole code (time available vs. time squeezed by a job, care or deadline) rather than a separate code. The claim is about women/mothers generally but is made in an entrepreneurship context and carries over to founders.

full_read_priority2.quote: In the absence of slack, these ideas are likely to stay undeveloped for a longer period of time or not be developed at all (in the same way employees at a firm may have ideas about improving a product or service, but may not have the time and resources to develop them until they are offered the opportunity to do so in a structured way).
full_read_priority2.in_context: Section 5.1.1 on shelving: during term (a competing commitment with high opportunity cost of time) students' project ideas stay undeveloped. Conclusion (p. 1070): 'In the absence of slack, projects that may have already absorbed time and resources through their ideation phase may never get developed further because teams cannot find the right time to execute on them.'
full_read_priority2.why: Theme not assigned to this paper; noted under step 5. States that a competing commitment (school work) limits time so that venture ideas slip or are never developed, and that less effort goes into each project when time is costly (model: e* = q/c_w). Same route as Markowska: the negative pole of condition-32.

themes.existing_code_overlap: trigger-10 'A personal misfortune' covers unwanted events (job loss, illness) and its rules exclude cases that only pushed the founder into the same work with no surprise. condition-14 'Motivation and incentives to act' covers a personal need, frustration or desire for self-employment that shapes acting on an opportunity. A welcome event or burnout that pushed the start is a motive, not a chance trigger, so it falls between these codes; condition-14 comes closest.
themes.summary: No held paper read in full states that a welcome life event or burnout pushed a founder to start; Reijonen and Heroum (2026) describe one founder who did exactly that after being worn out by her work, but as a case detail, not a claim. full_read_priority1.paper: Theunissen, Kensbock, Schüler, Baum & Gerards (2026) JOMS
full_read_priority1.quote: This transition can encourage mothers to rethink their career options, explore their values and priorities, and consider entrepreneurship as an alternative to wage employment (Caballero, 2017; Cai et al., 2019; Noseleit, 2014).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Preceded by 'Becoming a mother is a life-changing event (Stewart, 1982) that is considered to be one of the most sensitive periods for career decisions, identity reconstruction, and identity transition'. The discussion (p. 2493) restates: 'Motherhood can act as a liminal life event' that can encourage career exploration including entering entrepreneurship. The authors explicitly reject the necessity ('plan B', escape route) reading.
full_read_priority1.why: A welcome life event (childbirth) prompting a rethink that leads toward founding is the theme's idea, stated about would-be founders. Caveats: the sentence is a cited argument, the measured effect runs through leave time not the life event itself, it covers only motherhood (not burnout), and it frames the event as a motive and a source of time, not as chance. The theme is a motive, so it sits beside condition-14 (Motivation) rather than trigger-10; if coded, widen condition-14 to name a life transition as the source of the push, or tie it to Slack time when the event also freed time.

full_read_priority1.quote: When such change is unexpected, it may force an entrepreneur to resort to a hobby or moonlighting activity as a principal occupation in response to displacement.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Next sentences: the serendipity lies in the circumstantial change that recast the hobby; 'if the dramatic circumstantial change were anticipated, as in retirement from a career or a case of a person's vocation, the opportunity would fit better in quadrant III' (legacy, low serendipity). So Murphy covers an unexpected displacement (closer to trigger-10 misfortune) and explicitly says an anticipated life change is not serendipitous.
full_read_priority1.why: Sharpens the boundary rather than supporting a code: a welcome or anticipated life change that pushes the start is, by Murphy, low-serendipity (legacy), consistent with treating it under condition-14 (motivation) rather than as a chance trigger. Unexpected displacement that recasts a hobby fits trigger-10.

full_read_priority2.quote: For people, like the chefs interviewed here, hobby and leisure time provide a space in which to hark to and pursue an unanswered calling that may be missing from the workplace (Berg et al., 2010).
full_read_priority2.in_context: Full-time starters 'were unemployed or in a transitional phase when they started their full-time endeavors' (p. 197). The Figure 2 'Internal evaluation' codes include 'I knew I wanted to change' and 'Slowing down' (p. 194). The main push to start full time, though, is outside praise (diners, media, peers), not a life event.
full_read_priority2.why: Dissatisfaction with the day job, and a wish to change, are present as background motives, close to the burnout half of the theme. But the paper never names a welcome life event or burnout as what pushed the start, and job loss is a misfortune (trigger-10). The motive side fits condition-14 (personal need or frustration). The paper's stronger finding, that praise pushed the start, is better coded as trigger-24 or outcome-40.

full_read_priority2.quote: Parental leave acts as a trigger because it breaks behavioral patterns by allowing many women time and space to think about their own priorities and in so doing, reflect on their values, goals, and opportunities and act where appropriate.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Third contribution, Conclusion; preceded by 'we contribute ... by identifying parental leave as a possible trigger for women's career transition to entrepreneurship'. Life-story study of 18 Swedish mothers who founded ventures. Helena: 'Parental leave was a trigger' (p. 1186). Lit review p. 1171: 'Specific events, such as childbirth, are transitional moments that prompt individuals to reconsider their roles ... and their careers'.
full_read_priority2.why: A welcome life event (childbirth and the leave that follows) is named as the trigger for founding, and the paper insists it is not necessity or misfortune ('Plan A', not 'Plan B'). This is exactly the gap between trigger-10 (misfortune only) and drafted condition-14 (motive). Caveat for coding: the paper stresses that the women deliberately timed the start to the welfare rules, so the code is a non-chance push/occasion code, not a chance trigger; career burnout is not covered (Helena's dissatisfaction with career prospects is the nearest).

full_read.in_context: Both quotes are exact, but read in context they argue the opposite way from the claim. The paper is about COVID-19 as a sudden, extreme, low-probability shock and positions itself against earlier external-enabler work on slow, predictable change. Slow change is mentioned only as what prior literature covered; the paper says nothing about how gradual change acts on ventures, and gives no account of it as a distinct kind of enabler. It also notes onset (predictability and suddenness) as a dimension of enablers (p. 1, p. 2, citing Davidsson et al., 2020). Crucially for a chance code, the paper describes the slow changes as predictable and affecting ventures 'in imaginable ways', which counts against treating them as chance; and its own conclusion is that outcomes are 'not random' but depend on strategy. The paper's substance backs the existing code 'An outside crisis or disaster', not the new theme.

better_quote.quote: As an external enabler or disabler, a crisis varies in its scope of change (spatial, temporal, etc.) and onset (predictability and suddenness), which determine how the external changes, through various mechanisms, shape the roles and effects of a crisis

full_read.distinct: Closest existing code: 'An outside crisis or disaster' (the paper's own case). The paper only implies that slow change is a separate category in the literature; it does not make that case itself. Its 'relatively predictable ... imaginable ways' wording suggests a slow trend is not chance, so it argues against coding a slow trend as a serendipity trigger unless the founder's encounter with it was unexpected.

full_read.theme: A slow or indirect market change (Trigger)
full_read.page: e00514, p. 3 (sec. 2): 'defining the scope (i.e., spatial, sectoral, sociodemographic, and temporal) and onset (i.e., predictability or suddenness) of these changes' and 'roles specify broad impacts of mechanisms (i.e., triggering, shaping, or outcome-enhancing) on entrepreneurship'. Claim gave no page.
full_read.in_context: The paraphrase is partly wrong. The paper says onset means 'predictability or suddenness'; it never says 'gradual' (zero hits for gradual/slow). It does name scope including 'temporal', and the three roles, 'triggering, shaping, or outcome-enhancing', are exact. But these are a restatement of Kimjeon and Davidsson (2022), not the paper's own claim. The paper explicitly studies a short-term intensification of armed conflict as a triggering enabler (p. 3) and leaves long-term scope and the 'shaping' role to future research (p. 9). It does not say gradual or indirect change acts on ventures as a distinct kind of enabler. The indirect path it does test (conflict reduces FDI, which opens room for informal ventures) is an indirect mechanism of a sudden shock, which fits 'An outside crisis or disaster' rather than a slow trend. Its unit is country-year informal employment rates, not founders, and it says nothing about chance or the unexpected.

better_quote.quote: This may include not only the triggering role of armed conflict but also its role in shaping venture offering, processes and outcomes.

full_read.distinct: Closest existing code: 'An outside crisis or disaster' (armed-conflict intensification is a sudden, widely shared shock). The framework sentence (onset; triggering vs shaping roles) gives a vocabulary for separating a shaping background change from a triggering shock, which is what the theme needs, but the paper does not apply it to slow change and does not connect it to chance. Combined with Klyver & Nielsen, the literature support is for the dimension (onset, role), not for slow change as a serendipity trigger.

full_read_priority1.quote: Not all enablers qualify as sudden environmental jolts (Bradley, 2015) or other punctuated events; some, like climate change and most social movements, develop in a slow and measured manner.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Onset of external enablers varies in suddenness and predictability (Figure 3: aging population and social movements are gradual). External enablers are changes 'that entrepreneurial agents creatively or serendipitously benefit from' (p.313), and they can play a shaping role, not only a triggering one: 'Seemingly negative shocks such as natural disasters, war, terrorism, and political upheaval can delay the venture, occasionally leading to pure cases of process-only enablement by fortuitously improving the timing of the introduction of a product' (p.321). Unit of analysis is the emerging venture. Covers the gradual shift and the disaster-that-shaped-the-setting parts; a supply source closing is touched only by the enclosing example 'shortages and limited competition due to outbreak of war' (Table 1, p.319). Boundary: an enabler must be a distinct, identifiable change, not a 'gray wall of non-change' (pp.322-323), which matches trigger-12's exclusion of a vague trend with no named change.
full_read_priority1.why: trigger-12 already cites davidsson2020 but limits itself to technology, rules or platforms; trigger-11 requires a sudden shared event. Davidsson supports widening trigger-12 (or a renamed 'change in the outside environment') to include gradual demographic, sociocultural, economic or natural change with a named change, and to allow a shaping role (the change shaped product, venture or timing rather than starting the venture). A separate new code is defensible but would overlap trigger-11/12.

full_read_priority1.quote: This calls for (5) more attention to variance in the onset of the changes as well as to gradual changes such as demographic trends.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Preceded by 'Further, the single instances studied frequently represent sudden, external shocks.' Definitions p.653: 'For example, environmental disasters are sudden while environmental degradation is gradual, and patent expiry is predictable while introduction of new, disruptive technology is less so.' Roles p.656: 'Both anticipated and unanticipated mechanisms can enhance the outcomes', and EE mechanisms can shape product, venture or process (shaping found in 60 of 94 studies). Review of new-venture studies, so it carries over to founders. Adds 'indirect' enablement: non-business regulatory change offers 'nonobvious, yet effective enablement' (p.649). The framework still requires a distinct aggregate-level change (Table 2, p.649).
full_read_priority1.why: Same as Davidsson et al. 2020: supports widening trigger-12 to gradual and indirect outside changes with a shaping role. Kimjeon & Davidsson also show the evidence base for gradual onset is thin (3 studies, Table 4), worth noting in the code's source note.

full_read_priority1.quote: Through the mechanisms described below, we argue that media discourse may "nudge" the nascent entrepreneur into founding a firm (Thaler and Sunstein 2008).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Rising media talk about a technology sector (a trend, not a named event) raises founding rates in that sector over the next six months.
full_read_priority1.why: It shows a diffuse trend (media buzz) acting on founding, which is the 'vague trend' that trigger-12 excludes. But the theme is about a slow shift that shaped the setting rather than starting the venture, and here the trend starts ventures. The evidence is aggregate, not founder accounts.

full_read.in_context: The quote is exact but sits on p. 323, under 'Synchronicity > Mindfulness'. That section is about organizational design (creative compartments, autonomy), not an individual founder's disposition. Elsewhere the paper says serendipity involves 'prepared, curious and open-minded people' (p. 320). It also quotes Van Andel's untested list of serendipitist traits (p. 325). better_quote.quote: All these accidental discoveries suggest that serendipity involves prepared, curious and open-minded people acting on the world and finding some relation of knowledge and material possibility, the potential knowledge of which was always there, which others in their society had failed to realize.

Also cites Agarwal (2015)'s definition with 'a naturally alert actor' (ms p.5) and Bates' 'passive awareness' (ms p.7). None has the person name appreciative noticing as a source of power, and none concerns founders.

quotes.quote: Thus, I distinguish Mertonian serendipity where the discovery may lead to the solution of a given problem via an unexpected route, as distinct from the more traditional type of serendipity where the discovery leads to the solution of an entirely di ﬀerent problem.

themes.existing_code_overlap: type-01 'Mertonian: sought, found unexpectedly' (goal unchanged, met by an unexpected route) covers the type of this episode, and mechanism-28 'Perseverance and effort' covers the long run of failures. No trigger code names a surprise inside the founder's own results: trigger-04 needs an accident, trigger-05 needs a failure reused elsewhere, trigger-06 needs a side effect, and trigger-24 needs an outside market signal. So the gap is real but narrow (1 case); coding type-01 plus mechanism-28 may be enough.
themes.summary: Yaqub (2018) states the idea for science: Ehrlich found Salvarsan as the 606th preparation after 605 failed ones, solving the problem he was working on by an unexpected route (trial and error), and Yaqub counts this as Mertonian serendipity. In the codebook, 'Mertonian: sought, found unexpectedly' and 'Perseverance and effort' already capture most of it, so a new trigger code earns its place only if more cases like this appear.

full_read.in_context: The quotes are paraphrased. The Salvarsan sentence is 'Salvarsan was the 606th preparation, the 605 before it having each gone through their own set of experiments' (p. 169). It does not say they 'failed'. The Daguerre/Ehrlich ('Elrich') sentence is close to the original (p. 169). Yaqub uses both cases, plus Goodyear's decade of searching (pp. 170, 176), to define Mertonian serendipity: 'Targeted search solves problem-in-hand via unexpected route' (p. 170). He places the unexpectedness in the route, not the finding (p. 175). Error, spillage or trial and error is the mechanism. So this is serendipity in the Mertonian sense, but persistence and 'success after many failures' is not the point. The setting is science and technology, with only a passing note about entrepreneurship (p. 176).

better_quote.quote: Thus, I distinguish Mertonian serendipity where the discovery may lead to the solution of a given problem via an unexpected route, as distinct from the more traditional type of serendipity where the discovery leads to the solution of an entirely different problem.

full_read.distinct: Not distinct. This is the existing type-01 'Found what they sought, by an unexpected route'. A trigger version would duplicate type-01. Where an accident made the experiment work, it also overlaps trigger-04 'A mistake or accident'. Yaqub gives no separate category for 'own results finally worked'.

full_read_priority1.quote: They can 'break the mold' of what is familiar, even to the extent that they are astounding to the entrepreneurs who discovered them through their own efforts.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Describes the 'eureka' quadrant (high deliberation, high serendipity): an opportunity reached through the founder's own deliberate search whose scope turns out surprising. Also p.366: 'Opportunities can entail high levels of deliberation and serendipity based on the emergence of new information during search activity.' Conceptual paper, about entrepreneurs' opportunity formation, so it carries over to founders. But the surprise Murphy names is the unexpectedly large scope of what the search yields, not a long-failing attempt that abruptly works; no mention of repeated failure or of the surprise lying in the founder's own results.
full_read_priority1.why: Supports coding such an episode as type-01 (sought, found unexpectedly) plus mechanism-28 (perseverance); Murphy's eureka quadrant could be cited as an extra source for type-01 or definition-04 (high deliberation does not rule out serendipity). Not enough for a new trigger code.

themes.existing_code_overlap: trigger-11 (outside crisis) excludes events that hit only this venture, and trigger-10 (personal misfortune) is about the founder's own life. Closest are trigger-09 (unexpected obstacle during development), to which trigger-08's not-when already sends 'a technical, partner or customer surprise during venture development', and outcome-30 (harm or loss) for the result. A setback from one outside party could be handled by widening trigger-09 to name lawsuits, fraud and failing carriers or contractors, rather than by a new code.
themes.summary: Kosmynin and Ljunggren (2023), now held and read, give a clear case of one outside party (a partner municipality) unexpectedly ending a venture's resourcing, but they generalise only to 'unexpected situations', not to setbacks from a single outside party. No held paper states the idea as a general claim; Zheng and Mai (2013) on negative surprises in startups is the best paper to get.

full_read_priority1.quote: In this study, the Conspiracy narrative was used by those who sought to blame the self-interested behaviour or incompetence of certain project partners.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Definition of the Conspiracy narrative type; Table 3 also has a Zeitgeist quote, 'people (R&D partners) leave in the middle of the project; people just disappear and stop answering your emails'. Not assigned to this paper; noted under step 5.
full_read_priority1.why: It is about how blame is assigned in the telling, and the blamed partners are inside the consortium. It does not set out a category of venture-specific setbacks from one outside party.

full_read_priority1.quote: These mundane issues, including manufacturing delays, quality concerns, and part malfunctions, incite what we label operational legitimacy threats—threats to a venture's legitimacy that originate within the venture and challenge claims relating to the venture's ability to deliver on its promised value proposition.
full_read_priority1.in_context: The paper's typology (Table 1, p. 4) has environmental threats (macro-level events such as industry stigma or boycotts), strategic threats (pivots) and operational threats (internal). Its case data mention a patent infringement lawsuit and a late-delivered laser (Tables 4 and 7, pp. 9 and 19), but these are folded into 'operational' issues and not theorized.
full_read_priority1.why: The typology defines its focal threats as originating inside the venture, and its only outside category is macro-level. A setback dealt by one outside party that hits only this venture falls between its categories, the same gap the theme found between trigger-11 and trigger-09. The paper confirms the gap but does not fill it.

full_read_priority1.quote: Financial misfortunes, which were related to financial problems resulting from non-foreseeable conditions, such as poor customer response or the collapse of previously established agreements, accounted for 25 failures (14% of the misfortunes) cited.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Sub-categories of 'misfortune' attributions. Table 2 (p. 86) example: 'A lead investor in the company's next round of financing withdrew unexpectedly, and there was not sufficient time to secure additional funds given the current business and economic climate.' The 'funding' sub-category (investors losing faith) also fits.
full_read_priority1.why: Gives instances of one outside party (an investor, a broken agreement) causing a venture's failure, but the 'misfortune' category lumps them with market-wide forces and timing. It never separates a single-party setback from a shared crisis, and it codes attributions of failure, not events in the venture's path. It supports naming investor withdrawal and broken agreements if trigger-09 (drafted) is widened. It does not support a new code.

full_read_priority1.quote: Extant studies have shown that a founding team member's exit often means the loss of important human and social capital for the continuing team (Bamford et al., 2006; Guenther et al., 2016).
full_read_priority1.in_context: In Team B the departing co-founders hired a lawyer: 'We received a letter from the lawyer of [Blake E] and [Bobby E] that involved legal threats against [Bart C] and me.' They also claimed rights to the code (Table 2). Footnote 5 says Team F lost a technology sale because a competitor moved ahead while the team was absorbed in the exit. The sample was chosen so that no outside crisis hit the ventures.
full_read_priority1.why: It states 'a partner who leaves' as a setback that hits only this venture, and shows ex-partners turning into a legal claimant. That fits the theme's partner and lawsuit cases. But the partner is a co-founder inside the team, not an outside party, and the exits are not framed as chance. Best use is as a source for widening trigger-09 (non-core; partner surprises during development) to name a co-founder leaving and legal claims, with role-23/outcome-30 for the effect. It is not enough for a new code.

full_read_priority2.quote: YYZmedia had two kinds of nemesis: a major investor and a subcontractor.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Nemesis narrative (Table 2: 'Blaming others external to the organization'), used by founders in 17.4% of their attributions. Next sentences: the investor withdrew just before the key product was done, and 'The subcontractor responsible for the technical development of the crucial software also failed to deliver on time... causing financial losses and slowing down software development.' Table 2 separates this single named outside actor from Zeitgeist (industry-wide) and Fate (non-human environment).
full_read_priority2.why: The Nemesis/Zeitgeist/Fate split matches the theme's boundary with trigger-11 (widely shared crisis): one outside party hitting only this venture. Caveat: the paper treats it as blame in failure accounts, not as a chance event, so it supports the setback category, not its chance status. trigger-09 is drafted (core false); widen it to name a failing contractor, investor withdrawal, lawsuit or fraud, and adopt it, rather than a new code.

full_read_priority2.quote: For these informants, skipping an entrepreneurial stage was the culmination of positive consumer feedback and unexpected external factors.
full_read_priority2.in_context: One chef 'unexpectedly lost his weekly pop-up space' and opened a full restaurant. Another 'took the leap to restaurant ownership after being caught by the health department for serving food out of his apartment' (p. 198).
full_read_priority2.why: These are two setbacks from single outside parties (a venue, a regulator) that hit only that venture and pushed it forward. The paper reports them as events and calls them 'unexpected external factors' and 'external opportunities', but it does not theorise setbacks of this kind. It supports naming lost premises and regulator action in trigger-09.

full_read_priority2.quote: Chinese entrepreneurs often have to deal with unexpected events such as breach of contract.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Sample section, explaining why China suits a study of surprises; the Beta Software case (p. 202) is a major client's 'surprising request' for a different operating system, 'patently outside the scope of the contract', and a founder says the environment did not allow 'other means' such as a lawsuit. A negative surprise 'often represents threats that the focal start-up must deal with to survive or continue operating' (p. 202).
full_read_priority2.why: Names an outside party's breach of contract and a client's out-of-contract demand as venture-level surprises founders must handle, which fits the theme's examples. But it mentions breach of contract only in passing, attributes it to weak institutions in the wider environment, and never separates a hit from one party from a widely shared crisis. Its Beta Software case matches drafted trigger-09 ('partners or customers do not behave as planned ... forces the founders to improvise'), so the paper supports adopting trigger-09 and widening its examples to contract breach, legal claims and failing partners, not a new code. Outcome side stays with outcome-30.

themes.existing_code_overlap: account-19 'Setback reframed as fortunate' is already in codebook v3.0 (sources Brownell 2024, Garud 2018, Ma 2002, Soto-Simeone 2021) and its definition covers retelling a setback as good luck, as learning, or as making one stronger. The round 3 cases look like misses of account-19 rather than a gap; Vough and Barker Caza (2017) can be added as a further source.
themes.summary: Vough and Barker Caza (2017), now held and read, state outright that people can turn a career setback into a growth story with positive consequences, which adds a fuller source to Brownell's conjecture. Since account-19 already names this idea, the open cases should be recoded to account-19 rather than given a new code.

full_read.page: 104 (the 'Overall, we explain...' sentence and the growth-based-stories definition both sit in the paragraph after the one that runs over from p. 103, checked against the p. 103 image)
full_read.in_context: The quote is exact. The paper IS about how setbacks are TOLD: a 'growth-based denied promotion story' is a narrative built through sensemaking, in which the setback becomes a chance to learn and grow (self-insight plus adaptation). The population is employees denied promotion. The authors argue the model may extend to career setbacks generally, including losing one's job, but say other setbacks bring different identity issues. Nothing in it concerns founders, ventures, luck or a setback that opened an opportunity. A growth story is 'I learned about myself and adapted', not 'it was a lucky break'. So the carry-over to founders is plausible, not clear.

better_quote.quote: others construct what we term growth-based denied promotion stories, in which they perceive the denied promotion as an opportunity to learn and grow in their careers.

full_read.distinct: There is no existing code for setbacks. The nearest are 'Credited to luck' (explicit luck attribution, not tied to a setback) and 'Told as if planned' (retrospective smoothing). The theme is distinct from both. Vough & Barker Caza back only the 'retold as growth' half, and only for careers. A source on founders or entrepreneurs is needed to back 'retold as fortunate or lucky'. Other usable sentences: 'we believe that individuals experiencing an array of setbacks will engage in sensemaking about the setbacks and, under certain conditions, will construct growth-based setback stories.' (Discussion, page unknown) and 'individuals may construct denied promotions as assets rather than detriments to their careers' (Conclusion, page unknown).

full_read_priority1.quote: Those transitioning well also exhibited a strong (high) proclivity toward linking the skills and knowledge they learned to their emerging career identities as entrepreneurs while coping with trauma.
full_read_priority1.in_context: 'Coping competence transference': founders recast the trauma as the source of strengths for the venture, e.g. Aaron: 'All that s**t that happened to me I would never take it back; I would never trade it ... I am what I am today because of the things that happened before' (p. 516). The paper is explicitly about self-narratives and reconstructing a coherent story of the trauma, so it qualifies as an accounts paper.
full_read_priority1.why: Not assigned to this paper, but it states the idea for founders' accounts: a setback retold as having made the founder stronger. That is already in core account-19 'Setback reframed as fortunate'; adds a further source for account-19 rather than a gap.

full_read_priority1.quote: This lack of success could be written off as a failure. But, considerations of performativity suggest that such 'misfires' are an essential part of the process (Callon, 2010).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Discussing Doganova and Eyquem-Renault's (2009) case of a venture (Koala) that failed to enrol partners for its business model and then pursued a new path after the iPhone. The reframing of failure as a necessary 'misfire' is the authors' theoretical claim, not a founder's retelling. Section 5.1 (p. 1184) adds that after ups and downs entrepreneurs re-plot narratives 'in light of changed circumstances'.
full_read_priority1.why: Theory-level reframing by the authors, not founders telling a setback as luck or as something that made them stronger. account-19 (drafted) already has better sources; this paper adds nothing for it.

full_read_priority1.quote: This temporal comparison allowed narrators to transform a previously negative story (past) into a positive learning experience (present).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Middle-of-hierarchy switches 5 and 6 (Inevitability to Catharsis), triggered by moving from past to present tense. The Catharsis type (p. 1623): 'By framing the failure as a learning opportunity, Catharsis narratives allowed actors to perceive the failure more positively by highlighting the benefits gained from experience.' A CEO's quote: 'I wouldn't describe it (project) as a failure, it has been a great learning experience.'
full_read_priority1.why: States the learning half of account-19 (a failure retold as a learning opportunity), and adds that the retelling can happen within one interview. It does not state the 'good luck' half. Same carry-over caveat as above (corporate R&D project, not founders). Supports making account-19 tickable; it does not call for a new code.

full_read_priority1.quote: However, through our reading we came to realize that in certain categories, newspapers were reporting 'positive' perspectives, or were applying a positive outlook to the effects of a failure on the individual and area.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Section 7.1.1 'Is failure good or bad?'. Its examples: 'In high-tech, failure isn't a stigma', and a failure described as 'a learning experience that many say is better than getting an MBA'. The framing is by journalists and communities about whole-venture failure.
full_read_priority1.why: Reframing a failure in a positive light is reported, but by newspapers at community level, not by a founder retelling their own setback as lucky or as a lesson. A weak extra source for account-19 at most.

full_read_priority2.quote: The first category from our inductive analysis accepts personal responsibility for the failure and portrays the failure episode as a learning experience.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Catharsis narrative, almost only used by founders; epigraph 'I got a business education worth 21 million because [of MobGame]'. Founders split an old self from a reborn, wiser self.
full_read_priority2.why: States the 'retold as learning' branch of account-19 at founder level; not the 'lucky break' branch. Catharsis also involves accepting blame, which account-19 does not require. account-19 is core false in v3.0; this is a further source for adopting it.

full_read_priority2.quote: Instead of letting themselves be burdened by failure, they turn failure into a positive learning experience, which helps them to work on their identity validation as entrepreneurs who are responsible and therefore add value to their profession and to society as a whole.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Transformation narrative; 'the failure becomes integral to a positive journey'; founder Tom: 'the failure just pushed me to a different road'. Discussion (p. 16): failure framed as 'not only a positive experience ... but is one that is necessary', a 'badge of honor'. Theory section (p. 3, citing McAdams 1996) notes an involuntary transition can be turned into an epiphany such as 'a lucky break', but that is general identity theory.
full_read_priority2.why: Founder-level evidence for the learning/made-me-stronger branch of account-19; the authenticity narrative ('Failure gives you a lot of freedom') adds a variant. Supports adopting drafted account-19 (core false) with Castelló as a source; not a new code.

themes.existing_code_overlap: Most parts are now covered: validation by outcome-40 (Proof of demand), legitimacy and referrals by outcome-15, press and unplanned uptake by outcome-28 (Unplanned spread), outage and lost reach by outcome-30 (Harm or loss), resources and help (including volunteer help from a chance contact) by outcome-13. Left over: goodwill from a community or client, cost savings, and rivals thinned by a crisis, which no held paper states as a result of chance.
themes.summary: No new held paper states goodwill, free promotion, cost savings or thinned-out rivals as a result of a chance event; Klyver (2025) and Engel (2017) still only lean on goodwill. The theme should be split: most cases fit existing outcome codes (outcome-40, outcome-28, outcome-30, outcome-13), and the goodwill remainder stays inductive.

full_read_priority1.quote: When used with the practice of humanizing the venture, normalizing setbacks and resolutions works to accumulate a reserve of goodwill (i.e., the dispositional legitimacy buffer).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Goodwill as a stock built up through deliberate founder rhetoric. Not assigned; noted under step 5.
full_read_priority1.why: Names goodwill as a venture resource, but as the product of planned communication, not of a chance event. It does not state goodwill as a result of serendipity.

full_read_priority1.quote: However, successful activation of enabling mechanisms is sometimes fortuitous rather than strategic.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Outcome-enhancing role. Table 1 (p.319) lists mechanisms that match two leftover parts of this theme: Conservation 'Reduction in the amount of resources required to perform an activity' (cost savings) and Demand substitution '... making competitive offerings perceived as less needed or attractive (negative substitution)' with examples 'legislation that bans or disadvantages competitors' market offerings' and, under Enclosing, 'shortages and limited competition due to outbreak of war' (rivals thinned). Read together, cost savings and weakened rivals can be fortuitous benefits of an outside change, but no single sentence states them as results of chance; goodwill is not mentioned.
full_read_priority1.why: If adopted, an outcome code such as 'Benefit from an outside change: lower costs or weaker rivals' would pair with the widened trigger-12; it does not fit outcome-13, -15, -28, -30 or -40. Evidence is assembled from two places, so 'leans on it'.

full_read_priority1.quote: Both anticipated and unanticipated mechanisms can enhance the outcomes.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Table 1 (pp.645-646) revised mechanisms include Conservation (cost reduction), Risk/uncertainty reduction '... or increase in the perceived uncertainty pertaining to competitors' offerings' and Legitimation '... or reduction in such acceptability of competitors'; p.654-655 names 'reduced cost for acquiring customers and technologies as non-obvious enablement'. Cost savings and weakened rivals are listed as enabling mechanisms, and unanticipated mechanisms can enhance outcomes, but no sentence ties them to chance as a result. Goodwill not covered.
full_read_priority1.why: Same as Davidsson et al. 2020; together the two papers make a stronger case than either alone for an outcome code covering cost savings or weaker rivals from an outside change.

full_read_priority1.quote: Even during a failed campaign, project creators can receive cues from the crowd about the market potential of their proposed products.
full_read_priority1.in_context: 1,595 failed Kickstarter book campaigns plus an experiment with 125 entrepreneurs. Pledges received in a failed campaign count as market validation. Validation predicts persisting and later Amazon sales rank, and works better than Kickstarter's 'projects we love' badge.
full_read_priority1.why: Validation as a result is already outcome-40 (Proof of demand, core). Stevenson adds that it can come out of a failed attempt and could be added as a source there. It says nothing about the leftover parts of the theme: goodwill, cost savings, or rivals thinned by a crisis. The setting is a planned campaign, not a chance event.

full_read_priority2.quote: She claimed continuous two-way dialogue fostered 'goodwill' with Gadget/S's backers which, in turn, created a vibrant forum for prospective backers to observe when making their funding decisions.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Goodwill and a 'vibrant community of supporters' (p. 982, conclusion: 'perhaps more importantly, generate a critical resource for a venture ... a vibrant community of supporters') are results of deliberate community engagement during a campaign. Backers also volunteered translations into 50 languages (Appendix C), which is a resource from strangers.
full_read_priority2.why: This names community goodwill as a venture result and as a resource, which is the leftover part of the theme. But the goodwill comes from planned engagement, not from a chance event. So it does not state goodwill as an outcome of serendipity. The volunteer help is already covered by outcome-13, and reaching the funding goal as proof is covered by outcome-40. The paper could be cited as a source for goodwill as a resource, but it would not justify an outcome code for chance.

full_read_priority2.quote: The findings suggest that popular blogs can help new ventures in marketing, and ventures can utilize the money saved from decreased advertising for other purposes.
full_read_priority2.page: unknown (section 7, Discussion and Conclusions, about p. 989)
full_read_priority2.in_context: Managerial implication: eWOM from popular blogs is a cost-effective substitute for paid marketing, which can run as high as 46% of capital raised.
full_read_priority2.why: Cost savings is one of the leftover pieces of this theme, and the sentence names it as a result of third-party coverage. It is the authors' inference, not a finding, and the coverage is not framed as chance (founders are told to court bloggers). The paper's other results (VC attention, referral substitute, better valuations) are already covered by outcome-15 and outcome-28. Goodwill and rivals thinned by a crisis are not mentioned.

full_read_priority2.quote: Early customers can send a strong signal to followers and can certify the quality of the firm's offering.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Introduction: early customers act as a signal and certification for later customers and stakeholders; the outcome measured is revenue.
full_read_priority2.why: The results it names (certification or legitimacy, word of mouth, revenue) are already covered by outcome-15, outcome-40 and outcome-28. It says nothing about goodwill, cost savings or rivals thinned by a crisis, which are the leftover parts of the theme.

themes.existing_code_overlap: trigger-18 (unasked-for offer) needs an offer made to the founder; trigger-19 (tip-off or introduction) needs information or a link given to the founder; outcome-28 (unplanned spread and uptake) covers the result (press, adoption) but not the trigger. Unsought promotion aimed at someone else's audience is still not named by any code.
themes.summary: No new held paper states that a third party or platform promoting a product on its own initiative is a chance trigger; Agarwal et al. (2023) still only lean on it. New leads on unsought coverage and platform visibility (Toepler and Velamuri 2025, Greenwood and Gopal 2015, Carare 2012) are abstract only.

full_read_priority1.quote: It also provides more room for luck and serendipity by highlighting that external enablers sometimes exert influence without the agent's awareness (Denrell, Fang, & Liu, 2014).
full_read_priority1.in_context: External enablers are aggregate-level changes from which multiple ventures can benefit (p.313), e.g. platforms as a technology enabler that can give a legitimation or demand mechanism. A single YouTuber, influencer or app store choosing to promote one product is a venture-specific event, not an external enabler in this framework. Nothing states unsought promotion by a third party.
full_read_priority1.why: No support. At most, the fortuitous outcome-enhancing role relates to outcome-28 (unplanned spread), which already covers the result; the trigger gap stays unsourced.

full_read_priority1.quote: For example, changes that are helpful only to a particular venture do not qualify.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Appendix on inclusion criteria; Table 2 (p.649) likewise excludes a 'Significant external instance for particular venture only' (example: one of the venture's first buyers wins a major government contract). Third-party promotion of one product is exactly such a venture-specific instance, so the EE literature explicitly sets it aside. Crowdfunding platforms appear only as resource or legitimation enablers (e.g. Kromidha & Robson 2016 in Table A2).
full_read_priority1.why: No support; the EE literature excludes venture-specific events, so it cannot source this trigger.

full_read_priority1.quote: Specifically, we show that it is not the intensity and frequency of interactions (number of users' posts), but the positive response of the online community (reactions and comments of appreciation generated by users' posts) having the potential to favor the transition from pure leisure passion towards entrepreneurial intentions.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Endorsement here means likes and positive emoticons from forum peers on the creator's own posts. No third party or platform promotes the creator to its own audience.
full_read_priority1.why: The paper is about peer reactions to one's own content, not unrequested promotion by an influencer or platform.

full_read_priority1.quote: On one hand, the presence of firm-specific discourse in media has been argued to legitimize topics, industrial sectors, and firms (Pollock and Rindova 2003), thereby conferring superior legitimacy and reputation on the recipients of such discourse (DiMaggio and Powell 1983).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Panel of VC-backed US IT foundings 1998-2007 against changes in newspaper and blog mentions of each IT subsector. Coverage is counted at sector level, and its effect is on how many firms get founded, not on a given firm's sales. The paper even names the opposite case, founders who use their contacts to get coverage of their own technology (endogeneity section).
full_read_priority1.why: It cites the idea that media attention gives legitimacy to the firms it covers (Pollock & Rindova 2003). Its own evidence is sector-level buzz nudging people to found firms, not a third party promoting one product unasked. Neither trigger-18 nor trigger-19 is sharpened by it. outcome-28 (press as an outcome) already covers the result side.

full_read_priority2.quote: A good review in a local newspaper or celebrative Yelp evaluations can trigger a reframing of motivations.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Press (Chronicle, New York Times) and other chefs calling turned an 'amateurish movement' into a business (Restaurant chef #11, p. 197).
full_read_priority2.why: Unprompted reviews act as a trigger here, but the paper does not separate sought from unsought coverage or call it unexpected. Its effect is on identity, so it fits outcome-28 or trigger-24 rather than a new trigger code.

full_read_priority2.quote: Blogs may direct VCs' attention to those they select for coverage, thus increasing the exposure of ventures.
full_read_priority2.page: unknown (section 3.1, about p. 979; extraction has no page markers)
full_read_priority2.in_context: Signalling argument for H1A: bloggers choose on their own which ventures to write about ('Signals need not be broadcast only by firms; rather, any external monitor such as blogs can emanate signals for ventures'), and that coverage raises VC attention and financing. Popular-blog coverage is linked to higher amounts and valuations; Section 6 survey says VCs treat popular-blog coverage as a substitute for a referral.
full_read_priority2.why: Third-party coverage chosen by the blogger and aimed at the blogger's own audience is the theme's mechanism, and it is shown at venture level. But the paper does not treat coverage as unsought or as chance: it advises founders to approach popular bloggers and uses 'whether ventures have approached popular bloggers' as an instrument, so sought and unsought coverage are pooled. It supports a trigger distinct from trigger-18 (offer to the founder) and trigger-19 (tip to the founder); outcome-28 already holds the result. Not strong enough alone to source a new code.

full_read_priority2.quote: In addition to these lists, Apple facilitates product discovery by consumers through lists of featured products and, through the itunes program, staff favorite products.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Description of the App Store: Apple shows top-25/top-100 bestseller lists, featured products and staff favourites. Ranks are computed only from unit sales and developers cannot game them. The main finding is that the previous day's bestseller rank causally raises willingness to pay (about $4.50 at rank 1), with jumps at ranks 25 and 50 where the display pages break.
full_read_priority2.why: The paper shows a platform promoting a product on its own terms (lists and featuring) with a measurable demand effect, which matches the platform half of the theme. But it is about consumer demand, not about developers or founders; it does not separate editorial featuring from automatic rank display or measure featuring at all, and nothing frames it as chance. At most supporting evidence that platform exposure moves demand, under outcome-28.

full_read_priority2.quote: This premise is likely to hold because early customers are focal points that attract the attention of industry analysts, business press, and advertising agents as well as potential customers.
