full_read_priority1.quote: We show that the unexpected provision of unscheduled idle time affects individuals' creative performance at the idea-generation stage of the innovation process because the disrupted task remains active in their cognition.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Natural experiment in a manufacturer: a supplier fire stopped some production lines for four days; interrupted employees then submitted 58% more (and better) ideas for about three weeks. Planned breaks (long weekends, school holidays) gave no gain and intrusions (flood clean-up) lowered ideas. The mechanism is attention residue: idle time lets the interrupted work task incubate. Ideas are about the same work task, not a new outside input.
full_read_priority1.why: Strongest held evidence that unplanned idle time (not planned leave) helps new ideas, which is exactly the slack-versus-unplanned-latitude split drafted as condition-33 vs condition-32. But the subjects are factory employees, the effect is incubation on the interrupted task rather than room for an unrelated chance input or time to act, and nothing concerns founders or ventures. So it leans on the theme; it is better used to sharpen condition-33 (unplanned stoppage gives incubation time) than to support a new code.

full_read_priority1.quote: In this paper, we draw upon two plausibly exogenous shocks to an entrepreneur's free time: (random) injury and the 2011 amendments to Illinois's workers' compensation laws.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Difference-in-differences on zip-code new business registrations, Illinois vs Indiana, 2007-2016: after the 2011 reform cut workers' compensation (money and time off work), Illinois registrations fell about 31-39%. Authors argue that time to convalesce lets injured workers 'explore potential upsides of entrepreneurial activity without necessarily sacrificing wage employment' (p. 362) and frame this as slack time as a determinant of entrepreneurship. Footnote 5 (p. 375) reports informal talks in which injury was 'the inciting incident to entrepreneurial activity'.
full_read_priority1.why: Treats an unplanned spell away from work as free time that enables venture entry, which is close in spirit, but the evidence is aggregate registrations, time and money effects are not separated, and the time is not linked to any chance input. The mechanism is inferred, not observed. Useful as secondary support that free time feeds venture starting; does not on its own justify a code.

full_read_priority1.paper: Theunissen, Kensbock, Schüler, Baum & Gerards (2026) JOMS
full_read_priority1.quote: We therefore suggest that extending the time component of parental leave gives mothers a protected 'time off ' that they can use to explore their careers and new business ideas.
full_read_priority1.in_context: Same H1 argument: leave time is a resource for exploring careers and business ideas; the policy implications (p. 2493) say longer leave gives 'the time needed to explore and act upon entrepreneurial opportunities'. The paper also quotes Markowska et al. (2023, p. 1170) on leave as 'time to identify new business opportunities' (p. 2471).
full_read_priority1.why: This is planned, policy-granted leave, which the theme's overlap note says is not covered and which Schweisfurth & Greul find does not boost ideas. It shows free time enabling opportunity search and entry, not a cancelled job or idle day making room for a chance input. Supports drafted condition-32 (allocated slack), not unplanned latitude.

full_read_priority2.quote: Third, our findings concerning parental leave as an enabler of entrepreneurship suggest that parental leave offers women an opportunity to break the behavioral patterns of everyday work, providing time to reflect, scan the environment, and plan/kickstart their new ventures.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Limitations and future research; the paper then asks whether 'any type of sabbatical or break from one's normal job' would have similar effects. Table 5 (p. 1187) defines 'time to scan the environment and identify opportunities' as time used 'to increase alertness to what is happening in the environment'. Discussion (p. 1194) adds that founders 'creatively-and serendipitously-benefit' from the leave as an external enabler.
full_read_priority2.why: States that freed time from work raises alertness and lets founders spot and act on opportunities, which is condition-32's idea at founder level. But the free time is planned, long and institutional (parental leave), not a cancelled job or idle day, and the paper does not link it to a specific chance input. Best used as founder-level evidence for adopting condition-32 (time away from routine work enables noticing and acting), not as a separate 'unplanned free time' code.

full_read_priority2.quote: Given that the number of days that a college cancels classes due to snow varies exogenously from year to year and city to city, the positive and significant coefficient is consistent with such random increases in slack time having a positive, causal impact on the number of projects produced.
full_read_priority2.in_context: Section 5.1.1, causal evidence: unscheduled snow closings (unexpected free days) raise the number of Kickstarter projects launched, as do scheduled college breaks (+45%). Endnote 4 (p. 1071): 'the arrival rate is likely to be higher during breaks, because there is more time to think about ideas'.
full_read_priority2.why: The strongest evidence held that an unplanned free day (a cancelled class) makes room for launching ventures; the population is student entrepreneurs, so it carries over. But the mechanism is lower opportunity cost of time for developing and launching projects, not making room for a chance input; chance encounters or cues are never mentioned. Supports adopting condition-32 and widening it to cover unplanned stoppages that give time to act, not a separate 'unplanned free time' code.

themes.existing_code_overlap: type-02 'Walpolian: sought one, found another' and definition-04 'Searching for something specific' cover the 'found a marketplace while searching for wholesale goods' case. trigger-23 'Gap left by others' errors or oversight' covers noticing an unserved need or price discrepancy. trigger-20 excludes finds made while searching for that kind of information. What is left (surprise at what was missing or what it cost during one's own search) is best coded as type-02 or definition-04 plus trigger-23, not as a new code.
themes.summary: Held papers state the general structure (Yaqub's Walpolian type; Kim et al. for consumers; Fiet on surprise within search), but none states that a founder searching for a product or price was surprised by a gap. The theme looks covered by type-02/definition-04 plus trigger-23; Erdelez on information encountering is the one source to get if a separate code is wanted.

full_read_priority1.quote: However, Erdelez (1995) study also concluded that 'unexpected aspects of information encountering involve both the accidental discovery of information that had not been sought and the discovery of unforeseen characteristics of information that had been sought.' (p, 146).
full_read_priority1.in_context: Section 4 on early empirical IE research; the next sentence links the second aspect to pseudoserendipity ('right destination, wrong boat'). 'Unforeseen characteristics of information that had been sought' is close to a founder searching for a product or price and being surprised by what is missing or what it costs. But it is library and information science about information users in general, not founders or ventures; it does not mention surprise at an absence (a gap) or a price, and it is a second-hand quotation of Erdelez 1995.
full_read_priority1.why: Fits the existing route in themes_r3 (type-02 or definition-04 plus trigger-23 for the unserved need). The idea of an unexpected property of the sought thing could sharpen definition-04's applies_when, but carry-over to founders is not clear enough to source a new code.
